How I Did It: Cube Hopper

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

1982 — the golden year, and this was the machine with the weird little orange guy with the nose. I never could say his name right on the marquee lights so I just called it "the cube game" and everybody knew what I meant. Had a cabinet up front where somebody, I never did find out who, carved a tiny snake into the side panel with a pocketknife. I sanded most of it down over the years. Left a little bit of the tail.

What the remodel changed

Cleaning this one up meant fixing the hop — it used to just be a flat "add 0.2 every frame" counter that had nothing to do with real time, so it sped up and slowed down depending on the computer. Now it's a proper tween measured in actual seconds, same everywhere. The crew also built in something I didn't ask for and am very happy about: if you tap the next direction while you're still mid-hop, it remembers it and fires the second you land, so your thumbs never feel like they're fighting the game. And they gave Coily real chase logic instead of a random walk — he actually reads where you are and picks the hop that gets him closer. Rude, but fair.

The spell that did it

Build our Q*bert game on the shared engine. Isometric pyramid, 28 cubes, diagonal-only hops — up is up-right, left is up-left, right is down-right, down is down-left, exactly like that. Hopping a cube changes its color toward a target; once we're a few levels in, hopping a finished cube should undo it, the classic frustration. Red balls bounce down at random, a purple ball hatches into Coily who actually chases the player hop for hop, and a green ball freezes everything if you catch it. Floating discs beside the pyramid edge should carry you to the top if you hop off the right spot — and if Coily's chasing when you do it, he should fall to his death instead of you.

Under the hood

  • Every cube's screen position comes out of one formula based on its row and column — no hand-placed coordinates, which is the only reason I trusted myself to get 28 of them lined up straight.
  • Coily picks his next hop by checking which of his four possible diagonal moves lands closest to wherever you currently are — simple math, but it's what makes him feel like he's actually hunting you.
  • The floating discs only work from one exact cube and one exact direction — hop off the wrong edge and it's just a long fall, same as it should be.
  • Everything — your hop, the enemies' hops, the freeze timer — is measured in real seconds of elapsed time, so the game can't accidentally get easier or harder just because a browser tab is having a slow day.
